1.2.d: Two or more independent clauses joined by coordination (and, but, or) or punctuation.
1.2.e: "It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen." (George Orwell, 1984)

1.3.d: One independent clause and at least one dependent (subordinate) clause.
1.3.e: "The boy stood on the burning deck, whence all but him had fled." (Felicia Hemans, Casabianca)

1.4.d: At least two independent clauses and one or more dependent clauses.
1.4.e: "He was an old man who fished alone in a skiff in the Gulf Stream and he had gone eighty-four days now without taking a fish." (Ernest Hemingway, The Old Man and the Sea)

1.5.d: Independent clauses joined by semicolons, colons, or dashes without coordinating conjunctions.
1.5.e: "To be, or not to be: that is the question." (William Shakespeare, Hamlet)

1.7d.d: Makes a statement or expresses an opinion.
1.7d.e: "Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation…" (Abraham Lincoln, Gettysburg Address)

1.7i.e: "What light through yonder window breaks?" (William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet)

1.7m.d: Gives a command, request, or instruction (see also 5.7.6).
1.7m.e: "Do not go gentle into that good night." (Dylan Thomas)

1.7e.d: Expresses strong emotion, surprise, or emphasis.
1.7e.e: "What a piece of work is a man!" (William Shakespeare, Hamlet)

1.7t.d: A declarative sentence with a short interrogative tag appended, reversing the polarity of the main clause.

2.1.d: Able to stand alone as a complete sentence.

2.2.d: Cannot stand alone; attaches to an independent clause, often introduced by a subordinating conjunction (because, although, when, if).
2.2.e: "as long as it stays inside the maze." (Margaret Atwood, The Handmaid's Tale)

2.3.d: A dependent clause functioning as a noun — subject, object, or complement; often introduced by that, what, whoever. An expletive it can delay it to the end.
2.3.e: "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife." (Jane Austen, Pride and Prejudice)

2.4.d: A dependent clause functioning as an adverb — time, place, reason, condition, concession, manner, or purpose.
2.4.e: "If music be the food of love, play on." (William Shakespeare, Twelfth Night)

2.5.d: A dependent clause functioning as an adjective, modifying a noun or pronoun; introduced by a relative pronoun (who, whom, whose, which, that) or relative adverb.
2.5.e: "the Grinch, who lived just north of Who-ville, did NOT!" (Dr. Seuss)

2.6.d: Functional roles within a clause: subject, verb, direct object, indirect object, subject complement, object complement, adverbial.
2.6.e: "I shot the sheriff." (Bob Marley — "the sheriff" is the direct object)

3.1.d: A group of words centred on a noun (determiners, adjectives, etc.).

3.2.d: A group of words centred on a verb, including auxiliaries.

3.3.d: Preposition + its object (usually a noun phrase).
3.3.e: "From there to here, from here to there, funny things are everywhere." (Dr. Seuss)

3.4.d: Group of words that modifies a noun.

3.5.d: Group of words modifying a verb, adjective, or another adverb.

3.6.d: Headed by a participle (-ing or -ed/-en), functioning as an adjective.
3.6.e: "…the child sleeping beside him." (Cormac McCarthy, The Road)

3.7.d: Headed by "to" + base verb; functions as noun, adjective, or adverb.
3.7.e: "To be, or not to be: that is the question." (Shakespeare, Hamlet)

3.8.d: Headed by a gerund (-ing verb form) functioning as a noun.

3.9.d: Modifies an entire clause; noun + modifier without a finite verb, carrying its own internal subject.
3.9.e: "So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past." (F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby)

3.10.d: A noun phrase that renames or explains an adjacent noun; essential (no commas) or non-essential (commas).
3.10.e: "Atticus Finch, a quiet and dignified lawyer in Maycomb, defended an innocent man." (Harper Lee)

4.1n.d: Names a person, place, thing, or idea (common, proper, countable, uncountable, collective, abstract).

4.1v.d: Expresses an action, state, or occurrence (main, auxiliary, modal; transitive, intransitive; finite, non-finite).

4.1adv.d: Modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb.

4.1pron.d: Replaces a noun (personal, possessive, reflexive, relative, demonstrative, indefinite, interrogative, reciprocal).
4.1pron.e: "What light through yonder window breaks?" (Shakespeare — interrogative)

4.1prep.d: Shows a relationship between a noun/pronoun and other words.

4.1conj.d: Joins words, phrases, or clauses (coordinating, subordinating, correlative).

4.1det.d: Introduces and specifies a noun (a, an, the, this, some…).

4.3.1.d: Base form (3rd-person singular adds -s): habits, facts, timeless truths.

4.3.2.d: am/is/are + -ing: actions happening now, temporary situations.

4.3.3.d: have/has + past participle: actions with present relevance.

4.3.4.d: have/has been + -ing: started in the past and continuing.

4.3.5.d: -ed or irregular form: completed actions at a specific past time.
4.3.5.e: Narrative default: "…the clocks were striking thirteen." context

4.3.6.d: was/were + -ing: ongoing or background actions in the past.
4.3.6.e: "He was an old man who fished alone…" (Hemingway) context

4.3.7.d: had + past participle: an action completed before another past action (backshifting).
4.3.7.e: "She had gone eighty-four days now without taking a fish." (Hemingway)

4.3.8.d: had been + -ing: ongoing action before another past point.

4.3.9.d: will + base (or be going to): predictions, decisions, planned future.

4.3.10.d: will be + -ing: in progress at a future time.

4.3.11.d: will have + past participle: completed before a future point.

4.3.12.d: will have been + -ing: duration up to a future point.

4.4.1.d: Indefinite a/an for non-specific singular countables; definite the for known nouns; zero article for general plurals/uncountables.

4.4.2.e: "This above all: to thine own self be true." (Hamlet)

4.4.3.d: my, your, his, her, its, our, their — ownership or relationship.

4.4.4.d: Expresses amount or number: much/many/a lot of; little/few; all/some/any/no; each/every.
4.4.4.e: "A person's a person, no matter how small." (Dr. Seuss)

4.4.5.d: Cardinal and ordinal numbers are classified as quantifiers/determiners, not adjectives: they precede true adjectives, cannot be graded, and cannot be predicative.
4.4.5.e: "Four score and seven years ago…" (Lincoln) / "…eighty-four days…" (Hemingway)

4.5.d: A small word (up, off, out…) forming a phrasal verb whose meaning is not the sum of its parts; particles can move past a noun object and must follow a pronoun object.
4.5.e: "Never gonna give you up, never gonna let you down." (Rick Astley)

5.1.1.d: Subject and verb must agree in number and person.

5.1.2.d: Pronouns agree with their antecedents in number, gender, and person.

5.2.1.d: Opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose.
5.2.1.e: "a lovely small old round red Italian leather handbag"

5.3.1.d: Elements in a list, comparison, or coordinated structure must share grammatical form.
5.3.1.e: "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times…" (Dickens)

5.3.2.d: The subject may be omitted when clear from context — common in imperatives and compounds.

5.3.3.d: The subordinator "that" may be omitted before a nominal dependent clause.
5.3.3.e: "Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again." (du Maurier, Rebecca)

5.3.4.d: "There" as dummy subject asserting existence; the notional subject follows the verb and controls agreement.
5.3.4.e: "There was no possibility of taking a walk that day." (Charlotte Brontë, Jane Eyre)

5.5.1.d: Subject receives the action: be + past participle (+ by-agent).
5.5.1.e: "The cat was chased by the dog."

5.5.2.d: Modal verbs express necessity, possibility, permission, ability (can, could, may, might, must, should…).

5.6.1.d: not, n't, never, no reverse meaning; negating a main verb requires do-support.
5.6.1.e: "I do not like green eggs and ham." (Dr. Seuss)

5.6.2.d: Two negatives make a non-standard positive in standard English.

5.7.1.d: Special verb forms for hypothetical, wished, or suggested situations.
5.7.1.e: "…as if she were the sun…" (Tolstoy, Anna Karenina)

5.7.2.d: Splits information for emphasis with "it is/was" or "what".
5.7.2.e: "It was the dog that barked loudly."

5.7.5.d: Reversed subject–verb order for questions, emphasis, or after negative adverbs.
5.7.5.e: "Never have I seen such a beautiful sunset."

5.7.6.d: Commands and requests with implied "you"; may take flat adverbs.
5.7.6.e: "Do not go gentle into that good night." (Dylan Thomas)

5.7.7.d: Direct speech quotes exact words; indirect speech embeds them with backshifted tense and shifted pronouns.
5.7.7.e: "Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn." → Rhett said that he didn't give a damn.

5.8.1.d: Deliberate repetition of coordinating conjunctions for rhythm or magnitude.
5.8.1.e: "Think left and think right and think low and think high." (Dr. Seuss)

6.4.d: Capitals mark sentence starts, proper nouns, the pronoun "I", and titles.
6.4.e: "Toto, I've a feeling we're not in Kansas anymore." (The Wizard of Oz)

7.4.d: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma (splice) or nothing (fused). Fix with a period, a semicolon, or a comma + coordinating conjunction.
7.4.e: "It was raining heavily, we decided to stay inside." (incorrect)

7.5.d: A phrase or dependent clause punctuated as a full sentence — missing a subject, finite verb, or complete thought.
7.5.e: "Because the dog barked loudly all night." (incorrect)

7.6.d: A list or compound mixing grammatical forms (e.g. gerunds with infinitives). See rule 5.3.1.
7.6.e: "She enjoys reading, swimming, and to ride her bike." (incorrect)

7.9.d: Wrong subjective/objective case, especially in compounds or after prepositions.
7.9.e: "The secret is between you and I." → "…between you and me."

7.10.d: its/it's, your/you're, their/they're/there — the apostrophe form is always the contraction. Test by expanding it.

7.11.d: more/most combined with an already-inflected form; one degree marker only.
7.11.e: "the most unkindest cut of all" (Julius Caesar — deliberate)
